scenes.narration: Your computer knows the I P address it wants to reach. But the switch only understands M A C addresses. So how does it find the match? It asks.

lines.t: You know the I P address
The switch needs a M A C

scenes.heading: The office directory
scenes.narration: Picture a big office with no central directory. Everyone keeps a personal notebook of who sits where. Bob wants to send Alice a document, but he only knows her name. So he shouts down the hallway. Who is Alice? Please tell me your office number. That shout is the A R P request, and everyone hears it. Alice answers Bob directly, just to him. Bob writes it in his notebook, and next time he doesn't need to shout.

scenes.heading: Request and reply
scenes.narration: It's a two step conversation. First, a broadcast asking who owns the address. Second, a direct reply with the answer. Then the answer is cached for later.

scenes.heading: Useful commands
scenes.narration: Two commands to know. Show I P arp lets you see the cache. And clear arp cache empties it.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. A R P never crosses a router. It stays within one subnet. The reply is a unicast, not a broadcast. And cached entries do expire. On Cisco, after four hours by default.

items.right: It stays inside one broadcast domain
They time out (4 hours on Cisco)

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A R P turns an I P address into a M A C address on the same network. The request is a broadcast, and the reply goes straight back. Answers are cached, so it doesn't have to ask again. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva ARP lab.

points.t: ARP: IP address to MAC address, same subnet
